clinicalPearls: A palpable metastatic nodule at the umbilicus, signifying spread from an intra-abdominal or pelvic malignancy
Presents as a firm, sometimes ulcerated or discharging periumbilical mass that may be the first sign of an occult cancer
The commonest primary sites are the stomach, followed by other gastrointestinal tumours (colon, pancreas) and, in women, ovarian and other gynaecological cancers
Named after the surgical assistant who noted the association between umbilical nodules and intra-abdominal malignancy
Its presence indicates advanced, usually disseminated, disease and carries a poor prognosis
Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy or fine-needle aspiration of the nodule, which can also suggest the primary source
Management is directed at the underlying malignancy and is generally palliative, with treatment guided by tumour type and stage
reference.pathophysiology: The Sister Mary Joseph nodule represents metastatic seeding of the umbilicus from an intra-abdominal or pelvic primary tumour. Malignant cells are thought to reach the umbilicus by several routes, including direct extension through the anterior abdominal wall, lymphatic spread along embryological remnants, haematogenous dissemination, and contiguous spread along the obliterated umbilical vessels and the urachal or falciform ligament remnants. Its appearance therefore reflects transcoelomic or lymphovascular dissemination of an advanced cancer to the umbilical region.
additionalDifferentials: Primary skin tumour of the umbilicus
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy or fine-needle aspiration of the umbilical nodule for histological and immunohistochemical characterisation
Cross-sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to identify the primary tumour and stage disease
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy to seek a gastrointestinal primary
Pelvic imaging and gynaecological assessment in women
Tumour markers guided by the suspected primary
Positron emission tomography in selected cases to map disease extent
redFlags: A new firm or ulcerated umbilical nodule in an adult, which mandates urgent evaluation for malignancy
Associated ascites, weight loss, or a palpable abdominal mass indicating disseminated disease
Bleeding or discharge from the nodule
reference.prognosis: The nodule signifies advanced malignancy with peritoneal or systemic dissemination and is associated with a poor prognosis and short median survival, although outcome varies with the primary tumour type and response to systemic therapy.
pitfalls: Mistaking the nodule for a benign umbilical lesion such as a hernia or granuloma and delaying diagnosis
Biopsying without a systematic search for the primary tumour
Assuming a single tumour type when several intra-abdominal and pelvic primaries are possible
Overlooking the nodule as the presenting sign of an otherwise occult cancer
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Identify and treat the underlying intra-abdominal or pelvic primary malignancy, as the nodule is a metastatic marker and management is directed at the cancer
Confirm with biopsy or fine-needle aspiration and immunohistochemistry to characterise the tumour and identify the primary source
Systemic anticancer therapy, including chemotherapy and targeted agents, appropriate to the primary tumour and stage
Palliative local measures for a symptomatic nodule with ulceration, discharge or pain, including local excision or radiotherapy
Coordinated oncology multidisciplinary care given advanced, often disseminated disease
Early palliative care involvement for symptom control and supportive management
